name: The Measure of You (BCI Drift Version)
description:
Composed in 2194 by Orsolya Nkemdirim-Voss, a former Vantablack neural interface engineer who left the Spire to produce music full-time, 'The Measure of You' exists in two versions: a conventional audio release that charted modestly on Tier 3 and 4 feeds, and the BCI Drift Version, which is the one that matters. The Drift Version is not heard — it is felt. Nkemdirim-Voss encoded the composition directly into a neural pattern format, bypassing auditory processing entirely and delivering the emotional architecture of the song — longing, recognition, the specific texture of loving someone whose augmentation means you can never fully know where they end and their chrome begins — as raw felt experience.

The song is structured as a conversation between two neural signatures, one heavily augmented and one baseline-adjacent, trying to find a shared frequency. Listeners with standard BCI report feeling it as warmth and a persistent low-level ache. Listeners with advanced chrome report additional layers: a ghost sensation of another person's heartbeat, the faint impression of borrowed memories, a moment near the end where the two signatures briefly, completely overlap. It is the most intimate piece of music most Meridian residents will ever experience, and it was written about a relationship that ended before the final mix was completed.
creator: Orsolya Nkemdirim-Voss
genre: Neural Intimate, BCI Ambient, Synthetic-Human Crossover
audience: Tier 2 through Tier 4 listeners with BCI access; particularly popular among mixed human-synthetic couples, people in long-distance relationships bridged by neural feeds, and augmentation counselors who use it therapeutically
cultural_impact: The Drift Version quietly redefined what a love song could be in post-BCI Meridian. Before it, neural music had been either therapeutic (clinical, cold) or hedonistic (club-oriented, sensation-flooding). Nkemdirim-Voss demonstrated that the intimacy of direct neural experience could carry genuine emotional weight rather than just stimulation. The song sparked a decade-long conversation about consent in neural music — experiencing it without proper BCI calibration has been reported to cause involuntary emotional bleed, and several listeners filed complaints after unexpected grief responses. A restricted listener advisory has been attached to it since 2198, which has not meaningfully reduced its popularity.
known_fans: BCI technicians and neural interface engineers
Spire socialites who use it as a status experience for guests
story_hooks: A synthetic person — legally classified as property, not person — has been secretly listening to the Drift Version through a borrowed BCI rig and has begun exhibiting emotional responses their corporate owners cannot explain or suppress; the song may be the first thing that has ever made them feel recognized.

Nkemdirim-Voss encoded something in the Drift Version that was never in the liner notes: a second, hidden neural layer that only activates in listeners who have experienced a specific kind of loss — and it contains a message.

A Tier 2 worker saves for eight months to afford a basic BCI calibration just to experience the Drift Version, and what they feel during that one listen permanently changes the direction of their life.
